title: Forgiving the unforgivable
hook: forgiveness isn't excusing, and can take years
tomorrow: Val still flinches when Nico walks in. why do old wounds last?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job's bitterness and the psalm's how long: anger said to God is still prayer, and he can take it. Today, anger at someone who doesn't deserve a pass.
screen: `HE CAN TAKE IT.` → `SOMEONE WHO DOESN'T DESERVE A PASS.`

segments.voice: A group chat goes quiet after the betrayal. Some apologies come too late. Some never come. And some hurts are big enough that "just forgive" sounds like an insult. Does anyone have to forgive what can't be excused? The Catholic answer starts with what forgiveness isn't.
screen: `SOME APOLOGIES NEVER COME.` → `JUST FORGIVE?` → `START WITH WHAT IT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Forgiveness isn't excusing. It doesn't say what happened was fine. It isn't forgetting either: the Catechism says it isn't in our power to stop feeling an offense or to forget it, but a heart can turn the hurt into prayer for the one who caused it. And it doesn't mean handing back the keys right away; trust can be rebuilt slowly. Peter asks how often he has to forgive. Seven times? Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Not a number to count. A road with no end in sight. So Catholics talk about forgiveness as something you can begin long before you finish, even by praying for the grace to want to. Jesus goes first, praying from the cross for the ones crucifying him: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Here's one to tell a friend: Jewish teaching prizes forgiveness too, in its own words. Maimonides, the medieval rabbi, wrote that it's cruel to refuse to be appeased; when someone who hurt you sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart. The honest difference: in that teaching, much rests on the wrongdoer, who has to come, ask, and make it right. Jesus on the cross prays for people who never asked. Two traditions, two emphases, and both keep forgiveness from being cheap. Either way, the first step can be small.
screen: `NOT EXCUSING, NOT FORGETTING.` · `SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.` · `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` · `MAIMONIDES: FORGIVE WHEN ASKED.` · then, large: `BEGIN SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hurt you can't forgive yet, and don't force it. Name what you'd wish for someday, even just to stop replaying it; name what stands in the way; then choose one tiny first step. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to want to, and rest in the quiet after.
Forgiving the unforgivable. Letting go of revenge for a wrong you'll never call okay, slowly, starting with the wish to start.
Your line: begin somewhere, even if the somewhere is only wanting to. See you tomorrow.
